findings.headline: Over £360k in grant funding received but not yet spent may force a reserve drawdown if not expended in year.
findings.detail: The council received Crisis and Resilience Fund grant (£167,210), Renters Rights Act S31 grant (£60,000), Heating Oil CRF grant (£97,266), Asylum Dispersal Scheme grant (£37,200), and Adult Social Care Transformation funding (£12,803), totalling well over £360k. None of this had been anticipated in the Original Estimate. The paper states: "If not spent in year, this funding would need to be set aside in earmarked reserves for spend at a future date." This is a cash management risk.
findings.matters: Grant-funded spend that carries forward creates a reserve liability. If the council cannot spend this funding in-year, it creates a commitment that reduces future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Crisis & Resilience Fund grant income £167,210; Renters Rights Act grant £60,000; Heating Oil grant £97,266; Asylum Dispersal grant £37,200; Adult Social Care Transformation £12,803
findings.quote: If not spent in year, this funding would need to be set aside in earmarked reserves for spend at a future date.

findings.headline: Environmental Health externally sources statutory inspection work because the council has no qualified staff, and this overspend will repeat.
findings.detail: The council has zero budgeted for Environmental Health Consultants but has already spent £7,150 by end July. The paper states this is "Over budget as in previous years as the Council have no suitably qualified member of staff to carry out certain inspections which are part of its statutory duty." The action plan is to "Bring in budget at Revised Estimate" — meaning this is expected to continue. Flagged as a red variance.
findings.matters: A council unable to resource statutory functions internally faces recurring budget pressure and potential service risk. This is a structural problem, not a one-off variance.
findings.figures: Budgeted £0; actual £7,150 to end July; variance £7,150 overspend
findings.quote: Over budget as in previous years as the Council have no suitably qualified member of staff to carry out certain inspections which are part of its statutory duty.

findings.headline: Clitheroe Market maintenance is running 83% over budget four months in and is unlikely to recover.
findings.detail: The council budgeted £9,880 for annual repairs and maintenance of Clitheroe Market. By end July, £11,623 has been spent. The paper flags specific costs: £5k on a new roof for a market cabin, £760 on relaying unstable flags, and £2,340 on fire doors. The paper explicitly states "This expense area is already far exceeding budget early in the financial year. It is unlikely to recover the overspend as the year progresses." Flagged as a red variance.
findings.matters: Reactive maintenance running over budget suggests either deferred maintenance or an asset in poor condition. Either way, this indicates future capital or revenue pressure.
findings.figures: Budgeted £9,880 for full year; actual £11,623 to end July; variance £7,531 overspend
findings.quote: This is a reactive area of expensive with repairs being carried out as necessary. In the first part of 2026/27 a large amount (£5k) has been spent on a new roof for one of the market cabins, plus £760 on relaying unstable flags and £2,340 on fire doors.

findings.headline: Affordable rental housing is delivering no income four months in, due to delays in preparing properties and leases.
findings.detail: The council budgeted £17,270 of rental income from affordable rent properties in 2026/27. By end July, only £801 has been received. The paper attributes this to "longer than expected time taken in preparing the properties and leases"; repair works have now been completed and leases progressed with Onward Homes. The £7,835 shortfall is flagged as a red variance.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director assesses council balance sheets on asset productivity. Budgeted income from council-owned rental properties is not being realised, indicating either an optimistic budget or a problem with asset handover.
findings.figures: Budget £17,270 for full year; actual £801 to end July; variance £7,835 overspend
findings.quote: The longer than expected time taken in preparing the properties and leases means that an amount of the rental income budgeted for in 2026/27 will not be achieved.

findings.headline: Joiners Arms renovation abandoned; council considering alternative site due to building constraints.
findings.detail: The Joiners Arms Refurbishment scheme received quotes for renovation but these revealed the "location layout, and age of the building limits the size and accessibility of the units." The council is now considering alternative buildings entirely, with discussions underway with Onward Homes on a different site. Only £4,754 (1.9%) of the £250k budget has been committed.
findings.matters: Mid-delivery scope reversal and site changes suggest planning deficiencies in the original scheme design, indicating possible project management or capacity issues.
findings.figures: JARFB: £250,000 budget, £4,754 spent (1.9%), now considering alternative site
findings.quote: the location layout, and age of the building limits the size and accessibility of the units. Therefore, all options are being considered including alternative buildings

findings.headline: Purchase of Affordable Housing budget of £500k spent to only £26 with no committed schemes.
findings.detail: This scheme has spent just £26 of its £500k approved budget by end July. The monitoring report notes: "Options for spend are still being considered. Schemes with specific time restrictions have been prioritised." No specific affordable housing purchase has been identified or committed.
findings.matters: Undeployed budget for a core council service (affordable housing) at year mid-point raises questions about affordable housing delivery capacity and whether budgets reflect realistic delivery plans.
findings.figures: PAHSG: £500,000 approved budget, £26 spent (0.0%), £499,974 remaining
findings.quote: Options for spend are still being considered. Schemes with specific time restrictions have been prioritised.

findings.headline: Cemetery Extension faces High environmental risk requiring permit and multiple outstanding assessments.
findings.detail: The Tier 2 groundwater assessment identified a HIGH environmental risk score and concluded an environmental permit will be required. As of late July 2026, quotations for Biodiversity Net Gain, river, and ecological assessments were only 50% complete. Tender for development works (estimated £415,000) had not started, with August 2026 target.
findings.matters: Environmental constraints are delaying a £450k scheme and adding permit costs; suggests council capital delivery may face similar external blockers.
findings.figures: CCEME: £450,000 budget, £415,000 estimated development cost, £5,000 permit cost; £153 spent by 31 July
findings.quote: the calculated environmental risk score for the site is considered to be a HIGH and an environmental permit will be required.

findings.headline: Temporary Housing Scheme flagged RED and unlikely to complete in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The Temporary Housing Scheme (TEMPH) is only 25% complete on both planned works. The Wellbrow property works were delayed because the property remained occupied, and are now rescheduled to 31 October 2026. Waddow Green level-access works have not started. Both milestones were originally due within the financial year.
findings.matters: Slippage in temporary accommodation provision directly affects the council's ability to meet homelessness obligations and suggests delivery constraints on housing schemes.
findings.figures: TEMPH: £21,500 budget, £0 spent, 0% committed as of 31 July
findings.quote: Works delayed as the property has been occupied

findings.headline: Council is purchasing affordable housing using S106 commuted sums and expanding its housing stock.
findings.detail: Three properties in Longridge were purchased using S106 monies to be resold as affordable housing. The scheme involved higher acquisition costs than budgeted, requiring release of additional S106 funds (£51,336 variance) to complete the purchases.
findings.matters: Shows active capital investment in housing stock and asset acquisition, using developer contributions as intended.
findings.figures: Three properties purchased in Longridge; S106 variance of £51,336
findings.quote: S106 monies were released to support the purchase of three properties in Longridge to be resold as Affordable Housing. These had not been included in the budget due to uncertainty over scheme details or timings.

findings.headline: Council is closing Joiners Arms temporary accommodation for refurbishment in 2026/27 and preparing for higher homelessness costs.
findings.detail: Joiners Arms showed low occupancy throughout 2025/26. The council has explicitly set aside £20,000 from homelessness service underspend as a reserve to support higher costs in 2026/27 when the facility reopens after refurbishment. This represents both a capital requirement and a known service pressure in vulnerable housing provision.
findings.matters: It identifies a specific forward capital commitment and cost pressure in a key service area affecting vulnerable populations, requiring reserve management.
findings.figures: £20,000 reserve set aside; Joiners Arms had low occupancy throughout 2025/26 leading to lower utilities costs (£2,069 underspend) and equipment purchases
findings.quote: Due to the possible closure of the Joiners Arms for refurbishment in 2026/27 some of this underspend will be put in a reserve to support higher costs in this area in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Planning appeals driving unbudgeted consultancy and legal costs
findings.detail: The Planning Control & Enforcement service spent £38,068 more than budgeted on consultants and legal advice, with the overspend being largely due to appeals expenditure. The council is funding £21k from additional planning income and the remainder from earmarked reserves set aside in the previous financial year.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted appeals and litigation costs are consuming resources and drawing on reserves, which signals ongoing pressure on the planning service that could persist if appeal activity remains at this rate
findings.figures: £38,068 overspend; £21k to be funded from additional planning income; remainder from earmarked reserves
findings.quote: Consultancy advice and legal costs relating to planning applications have exceeded the budget for the period. This is largely due to expenditure on appeals.

findings.headline: The £4m Ribblesdale Pool refurbishment has already committed 95% of its budget by end Q1, with complex multi-year Alliance Leisure partnership dependencies.
findings.detail: The pool refurbishment scheme (£4m total) has commitments of £3.79m by end June, with work still in design phase. Alliance Leisure partnership agreement took 'longer than expected' to finalise and the full completion timeline remains 'TBC'. This is the single largest capital commitment in the programme with significant exposure to partner execution risk.
findings.matters: The council is heavily exposed to a major capital project dependent on external partner performance, with design-phase timeline slippage suggesting possible further delays.
findings.figures: £4,000,970 total budget; £3,789,782 committed/spent (95%); works completion date TBC
findings.quote: The work required to agree the contract with Alliance Leisure took longer than expected, due to the need to ensure the legal documentation was correct and satisfactory from the Councils' perspective, this is now complete and the surveys and design work is underway.

findings.headline: Heritage Lottery funding bids have failed, requiring emergency budget increases for two major schemes.
findings.detail: The Castle Keep restoration project (described separately as having cost pressures) and the Castle grounds improvements both had Heritage Lottery bids that were unsuccessful. The Policy and Finance Committee approved increased budgets in February 2025 as a result. The Castle grounds scheme now has an £1.8m budget with 'partnership engagement now underway for final submission' to Lottery, indicating a retry is planned but not assured.
findings.matters: Inability to secure external funding is requiring the council to fund schemes from its own capital, reducing flexibility and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Castle grounds approved budget increased to £1,792,380 after Lottery bid failure; Castle Keep also affected
findings.quote: Whilst a Lottery bid for additional funding was unsuccessful, Policy and Finance Committee in February 2025 agreed an overall increased budget of £1,792,380.

findings.headline: Two major capital schemes remain stalled pending Football Foundation match-funding decisions and have absorbed other dependent projects.
findings.detail: The new 3G pitch at Edisford (£1.4m budget) was originally meant to start spring 2025 but remains unstarted pending Football Foundation funding discussions to include additional pitches at Langho. This has cascaded to block the fence and gates project (£53k) which cannot proceed until the 3G pitch scheme is resolved and its layout confirmed. The fencing work is now not expected until 2027/28.
findings.matters: External funding dependency is creating schedule uncertainty and tying up capital budget allocations, delaying multiple related projects.
findings.figures: LRGAW £1,415,580 unspent; FGEPP £53,770 moved to 2027/28; two schemes on hold since spring 2025
findings.quote: The original aim was to be on site in Spring 2025. However, since discussions with the Football Foundation, and their proposal to help fund two further pitches at Langho and Edisford using the Council's allocation to match fund, the scheme has taken on a higher level of complexity and scale.

findings.headline: Vehicle procurement difficulties are delaying capital delivery and forcing service continuity workarounds.
findings.detail: Food waste collections capital scheme faced 'difficulties in procuring vehicles', delaying the operational rollout to February 2027. Paper collection vehicles are being sourced as second-hand units because 'one existing vehicle has a failed engine that has proved too costly to repair and urgently needs replacing'. A hire vehicle is being used temporarily, incurring additional costs to maintain service levels.
findings.matters: Supply chain delays and emergency vehicle replacements signal operational pressures and unbudgeted interim costs, affecting service delivery and capital efficiency.
findings.figures: Food waste rollout delayed to Feb 2027; paper collection vehicles at £63,000 each; hire vehicle costs for temporary cover
findings.quote: The introduction of food waste will now take place in Feb 2027 due to difficulties in procuring vehicles.

findings.headline: Engineering resource constraints are delaying capital projects and requiring external project management support.
findings.detail: The concrete bays replacement scheme at Salthill depot has been delayed until September 2026 due to 'engineering resources to manage the scheme'. The garage workshop refurbishment has not started for the same reason and is now being delivered by an external project management team. This indicates capacity limits within internal engineering capability.
findings.matters: Resource constraints can affect council's ability to deliver capital programmes on time and could indicate broader capacity issues in delivering services.
findings.figures: CBAYS (£20,280) delayed to Sept 2026; SHDRF (£232,150) not commenced
findings.quote: This work has been delayed until September 2026 with the contractor agreement. This is due to engineering resources to manage the scheme.

findings.headline: Castle Keep repairs have exceeded budget and additional works remain unfunded.
findings.detail: The scheme is already 106% spent (£548k of £556k budget) by end Q1. Additional lime repointing works were recommended in July by the Director of Communities, requiring emergency committee approval for further funding. The report notes that 'any further requests will be strongly challenged with consultant', indicating the council is managing cost overruns tightly but additional work exposure remains.
findings.matters: A major heritage scheme has already required additional funding approvals and faces further cost pressures, signalling either budget-setting issues or scope creep that could recur.
findings.figures: £556,400 approved budget, £548,424 spent/committed (106%), additional emergency funding approved, further works recommended
findings.quote: Additional funding through emergency committee agreed. Any further requests will be strongly challenged with consultant.

findings.headline: Grant-funded programs experiencing persistent deployment delays and unspent allocations
findings.detail: Food waste collection service delayed to Autumn/Winter 2026 (£10k promotional budget unspent); Smokefree Lancashire received £30k in December 2025 with £14,153 unspent by year-end; Sport England TaAF delivered 3 schemes instead of 4 planned; 6 approved recreation grant recipients had not claimed by year-end.
findings.matters: Repeated pattern of grant deployment delays suggests weak program delivery capacity or unclear requirements. Creates compliance risk if conditions are time-bound and financial pressure if grants must be returned or are reduced in future.
findings.figures: Smokefree Lancashire underspent by £14,153 of £30,000; food waste publicity £10,000 unspent; one fewer TaAF scheme deployed
findings.quote: There has been no publicity spend in-year as the service will not now start until Autumn or Winter 2026 ... £14,153 of this funding was unspent at 31/3/2026 and was set aside in the Exercise Referral (Smokefree Lancashire) Reserve at year-end.

findings.headline: Ribblesdale Pool closed in April 2026 with unclear replacement or revenue impact
findings.detail: Pool closed immediately after financial year end (April 2026). Multiple budget lines show variances attributed to shutdown: maintenance deferred, staffing adjustments made. The report gives no detail on replacement provision or whether this represents permanent loss of leisure capacity.
findings.matters: Closure of a material leisure asset represents a change to the council's service portfolio and asset base. Lack of narrative about replacement or impact on residents and community suggests planning gaps.
findings.figures: Ribblesdale Pool net underspend £28,705, largely attributable to reduced spend ahead of April 2026 closure
findings.quote: Less training costs in-year than budgeted for in the run up to the April 2026 pool closure ... Less demand for reactive building repairs work at the pool site in-year. There was less reactive maintenance undertaken in early 2026 in the run up to the April 2026 pool closure.

findings.headline: Play area capital investment delivered only 46% of budgeted S106 spend
findings.detail: Budgeted S106 developer contributions for play areas and pitches was £266,670; actual spend only £122,849, leaving £143,821 undeployed. This is not a one-year timing issue but indicates systematic underperformance in capital projects funded by S106.
findings.matters: S106 contributions have conditions and deadlines. Undeployed funding indicates either weak project pipeline or delivery constraints. Underperformance on capital raises questions about asset maintenance and community infrastructure.
findings.figures: Budgeted S106: £266,670; actual spent: £122,849; shortfall: £143,821 (54%)
findings.quote: At revised estimate budget stage it had been estimated that £266,670 of eligible capital scheme spend on play areas would be funded by S106 contributions. In practice, the Council actually spent £122,849 on play areas and playing pitches capital schemes that were funded by S106 developer contributions.

findings.headline: Multiple services dependent on aging, unreliable vehicles requiring expensive emergency hire
findings.detail: Transfer station overspent £8,456 hiring alternative equipment while waiting for replacement delivery. Refuse collection needed hire costs for vehicles off road. This pattern across services suggests systemic fleet aging rather than isolated incidents.
findings.matters: Fleet reliability failures create operational risk (service interruption) and financial risk (expensive emergency hire). Indicates underprovision for planned capital replacement.
findings.figures: Transfer station overspend £8,456; refuse collection vehicle hire costs included in £65,223 vehicle repair variance
findings.quote: High level of vehicle costs due to the need to hire alternative equipment whilst waiting for a replacement to be delivered

findings.headline: Refuse collection service overspent by £93k, driven by aging fleet and staffing shortages
findings.detail: Temporary staffing overspent by £17,153 due to unexpected sickness, vehicle repairs and hire costs overspent by £65,223 because vehicles were off road with mechanical issues, and wheel bin replacement overspent by £24,776 because bins are aging. These are not one-off variances but structural service pressures.
findings.matters: Refuse collection is a statutory service under pressure from fleet deterioration and labor availability. Rising replacement costs and mechanical unreliability indicate the council faces either fleet capital investment or sustained high operational costs.
findings.figures: Temporary staff £17,153 overspend; vehicle repair £65,223 overspend; bin replacement £24,776 overspend; net service overspend £93,076
findings.quote: The budget for temporary staff was substantially increased at the revised estimate. This has been exceeded even further and shows an overspend on the revised estimate of £17,153 ... There has also been a large overspend on vehicle repairs and maintenance costs. This is mainly due to hire costs while the vehicles were off road because of mechanical issues, plus increased mechanics time and costs of parts. The overspend reflects an increase in replacement bins issued, which is due to the ageing condition of many of the bins currently in use across the borough.

findings.headline: Ribblesdale Pool closed April–September 2026 for refurbishment; service and revenue disrupted
findings.detail: The main leisure facility is closed for four months for refurbishment works, with staff redeployed to other sites. This disrupts income (pool attendant vacancy underspend and low income) and creates temporary staffing overspends in grounds maintenance and street cleansing due to pool staff redployment.
findings.matters: Major service closure affects revenue and requires temporary operational adjustments; income loss from closure may exceed budget assumption if closure extends or uptake post-reopening is weak.
findings.figures: Pool attendants wages underspend £5,225; pool income expected to recover post-September; grounds maintenance temporary staff benefit from redeployed pool staff (underspend £11,451)
findings.quote: Less use of temporary staff has been required on the Grounds Maintenance team in-year so far because of extra input received from some Ribblesdale Pool staff that have been re-deployed to other sites whilst the pool is closed for refurbishment between April and September 2026.

findings.headline: Car park income weaker than expected across multiple sites
findings.detail: Multiple car parks running below budgeted income: Edisford (£5,637 shortfall), Chester Avenue (£2,248), Ribchester (£2,205), and Wellgate (£2,364). These are demand-led shortfalls against an annual full-year budget, suggesting structural weakness in car park usage or tariff acceptance.
findings.matters: Car park income is discretionary revenue that supports service sustainability; sustained underperformance across multiple sites signals wider demand issue rather than site-specific problem.
findings.figures: Edisford car park: -£27,224 budget to June, actual -£21,587 (£5,637 under); Chester Avenue -£10,252 budget, actual -£8,004 (£2,248 under); others similar
findings.quote: Lower than estimated demand for the use of this car park. Income for this cost centre will be monitored and cost centre reviewed at revised estimate and amended if needed.

findings.headline: Trade waste collection income declining; businesses seek all-in-one waste service the council cannot yet offer
findings.detail: Trade waste income is £6,520 under budget to June with the council experiencing declining customer numbers. The stated reason is that new food waste collection requirements mean businesses now prefer bundled collection from a single provider, but the council does not yet offer food waste for trade waste customers, causing them to leave.
findings.matters: Revenue reduction from a service the council is positioned to provide; uptake recovery depends on launching food waste collection for this segment, a capital-dependent change.
findings.figures: Full-year trade waste budget £394,740; underbilled by £6,520 to June; council acknowledges decline in customers
findings.quote: Budgeted income is lower than expected as the Council has seen a decline in trade waste customers lately. This is due to new requirements around food waste collections, currently the Council does not offer this service and businesses would prefer an all in one service where waste is only collected by one organisation

findings.headline: Public conveniences staffing: toilet cleaner vacancies forcing contractor hire after failed recruitment
findings.detail: Underspend of £27,499 on general cleaning reflects vacant toilet cleaner posts, but the council has made the decision to hire a contractor to maintain cleanliness standards after a failed recruitment process. Budget will be reviewed at revised estimate to reflect this change in service delivery model.
findings.matters: Failed recruitment forcing outsourced service model for basic amenity maintenance; suggests difficulty retaining or recruiting for lower-paid roles and indicates a structural shift in service model.
findings.figures: £27,499 underspend on cleaning labour to June offset by contractor appointment decision
findings.quote: To ensure Public Conveniences remain clean and tidy, the Council has made the decision to hire in a contractor to clean toilets due to a failed recruitment process.

findings.headline: Refuse collection temporary staffing overspend of £25,435 in six months with underlying vacancy
findings.detail: Substantially higher use of temporary staff to cover a driver vacancy in refuse collection. To ensure rounds are completed and schedule maintained, the council appointed agency staff urgently. This is flagged as requiring ongoing discussion between service and finance.
findings.matters: Suggests difficulty recruiting to permanent posts in this service, and implies full-year temporary staffing cost could reach £50k+, indicating structural staffing shortage.
findings.figures: £25,435 overspend to June; temporary staff budget for year £15,030; agency staff (separate code) £17,878 overspend
findings.quote: There has been a substantially higher level of use of temporary staff than the budget allows for. Discussions are continuing with the service area to address this variance.

findings.headline: Refuse collection fleet maintenance costs £39,632 over budget in six months, driven by mechanic vacancy and vehicle hire
findings.detail: The council's refuse collection vehicle fleet is running at significant cost overrun with major drivers being: hiring replacement vehicles whilst repairs are pending (£), outsourced workshop cover due to mechanic post vacancy, external technician input, and rising costs of genuine parts. The mechanic vacancy is preventing timely repairs, leading to longer downtime and more expensive remedial work.
findings.matters: Fleet maintenance is a core operational cost for waste collection; this trajectory suggests full-year overspend around £80k+, and creates service delivery risk if vehicle availability deteriorates.
findings.figures: £39,632 overspend to June (six months into financial year); net repairs across refuse collection vehicles budget £305,610 full year
findings.quote: The large variance is mainly due to the costs of hiring vehicles whilst repairs are being carried out on Council owned vehicles. Other significant costs include workshop cover from a third-party contractor whilst there is a vacancy for a Mechanic, procuring external vehicle technician input for some issues and the cost of authentic parts to repair vehicles with.

findings.headline: Landlord Tenant Grants scheme appears underfunded for actual demand
findings.detail: The Landlord Tenant Grants scheme had its budget cut from £162,440 to £35,000 at revised estimate (78% reduction), but actual spend was £47,852, exceeding the revised estimate by 37%. The council carried forward negative slippage of £12,850 to be deducted from 2026/27.
findings.matters: A scheme consistently underfunded relative to demand indicates either poor needs forecasting or demand that exceeds the council's current capacity to fund. Rolling schemes like this suggest ongoing demand that is not being met.
findings.figures: Revised estimate £35,000, actual expenditure £47,852, variance +£12,852
findings.quote: The budget was amended down at Revised Estimate based on predicted spend. Actual spend was in excess of the RE budget and therefore negative slippage is carried forward to be deducted from the 2026-27 budget.

findings.headline: Waterloo House Flat Scheme overspent its revised estimate by £39,790
findings.detail: The Waterloo House capital scheme had a revised estimate of £900,000 but actual expenditure was £939,790, an overspend of 4.4%. The council is carrying forward negative slippage of £39,790 to be deducted from the 2026/27 budget for this scheme.
findings.matters: A capital scheme overshooting its budget indicates either poor cost control or unrealistic initial estimates. The council is managing the overspend by reducing the next year's budget rather than funding the excess within-year.
findings.figures: Revised estimate £900,000, actual expenditure £939,790, variance +£39,790
findings.quote: Actual spend in 2025/26 was in excess of the RE budget and therefore 'negative' slippage will be carried forward against the 2026/27 budget for this scheme.

findings.headline: Purchase of Affordable Housing scheme deferred pending member consideration of best use
findings.detail: A £500,000 scheme with zero expenditure in 2025/26 is being carried forward in full to 2026/27. The stated reason is that the scheme has been moved pending member consideration of how the money should be used. No clarity on timeline or decision process.
findings.matters: A half-million-pound capital allocation cannot be deployed because the council is still deciding what to do with it. This represents both delivery risk and uncertainty about the council's capital strategy.
findings.figures: £500,000 revised estimate for 2025/26, £0 actual expenditure
findings.quote: Scheme moved to 2026/27 whilst options for best use are considered by members.

findings.headline: Clitheroe Market Improvements scheme stalled with members unable to decide on options
findings.detail: A £500,000 capital scheme approved in February 2026 has had almost no spend (£6,304 of £500,000) and is largely being moved to 2026/27. The reason stated is that members are still considering different options for improvement and have not yet decided the scope. No completion date is given.
findings.matters: A major capital allocation sitting in limbo due to lack of member decision-making indicates governance friction and capital deployment risk. The money cannot be deployed while the council decides what to do with it.
findings.figures: £500,000 additional approval 2025/26, with only £6,304 spent in year
findings.quote: The scheme has largely been moved into 2026-27 as members consider different options for improvement of the market.

findings.headline: Affordable Housing Longridge scheme abandoned due to S106 time pressure
findings.detail: The original £1m Affordable Housing Longridge scheme was ended and replaced by alternative schemes. The explicit reason given is time pressure to spend S106 (developer contribution) monies before their deadline expired. This indicates the council could not deliver the planned scheme within the required timeframe and had to change course.
findings.matters: The inability to deliver capital schemes within required timeframes (especially for externally-funded commitments like S106) signals delivery risk and potential future breaches of funding conditions.
findings.figures: £1,000,000 original estimate for 2025/26
findings.quote: This scheme was ended and replaced by alterative affordable housing schemes due to time pressures to spend S106 monies.

findings.headline: Mandatory NDR system update costs £7,997 following legislative changes
findings.detail: Unavoidable expenditure of £7,997 was incurred for a system update required to comply with English Non-Domestic Rates legislative changes. The council expects new burdens funding from central government to recover this cost.
findings.matters: Unfunded or partially funded legislative mandates reduce financial headroom; recovery depends on government timescales.
findings.quote: Unavoidable expenditure on a system update that was required following English NDR Legislative changes. New burdens funding is likely to be received from central government in due course.

findings.headline: Unforeseen civil matters push legal services budget £2,734 over estimate
findings.detail: The Chief Executives Department's legal budget has overrun by £2,734 due to several unanticipated civil matters requiring specialised professional legal advice. The paper does not detail what these civil matters are.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted legal costs often signal unexpected disputes, employment issues, or other governance challenges; unexplained legal spend is a warning signal.
findings.figures: £2,734 overspend
findings.quote: Requirements for specialised professional legal advice have exceeded the funds set aside in the budget for the 2025/26 financial year due to several unanticipated civil matters.

findings.headline: Council offices repairs budget overrun of £10,566 driven by staffing vacancies and reduced in-house maintenance capacity
findings.detail: The council offices repairs and maintenance budget has overrun by £10,566 to end February. £3,000 is an adjustment for unrecovered works team costs due to staffing issues, with the remainder being responsive repairs that exceed budget. The council is managing reduced capacity by hiring external contractors and has recently re-advertised a vacant position while managing long-term sickness absence.
findings.matters: Staffing vacancies in the works administration service force reliance on external contractors for building repairs, signalling asset management risk and rising maintenance costs that may continue into future years.
findings.figures: £10,566 overspend; £3,000 from staffing adjustment
findings.quote: £3k of the overspend is a charge from the works team due to an adjustment required because of staffing issues on the works administration service. The remainder of the overspend is the cost of responsive repairs. This will include the cost of hiring external services where necessary to undertake repairs that cannot be undertaken internally due to the reduced capacity set out above.

findings.headline: Ribblesdale Pool scheduled for 6-month refurbishment closure beginning April 2026 during peak season
findings.detail: The pool will close for refurbishment from April 2026 for 6 months (covering the peak demand season April-September). Pass sales are already tracking below budget as customers anticipate closure. Income variance shows £5,569 shortfall to end January, with council expecting under-recovery to persist through year-end.
findings.matters: The pool is a material revenue-generating asset. A 6-month closure during peak season creates a significant revenue gap. Council must manage both the capital cost of refurbishment and multi-month revenue loss during closure plus recovery period after reopening.
findings.figures: 6-month closure from April 2026; income variance (shortfall) £5,569 to end January
findings.quote: It is expected that this under-recovery of income will remain at year-end, because less of these swimming passes are being sold as we get nearer to the six month closure of Ribblesdale Pool in April 2026 for refurbishment works.

findings.headline: Wheelie bin fleet aging driving replacement spending 51% over budget by end of January
findings.detail: Budget for replacing obsolete and broken householder wheelie bins is overspent by £15,495 to end of January against a full-year budget of £30,000. Council attributes this to ageing condition of bins across the borough and expects the overspend to continue. If the rate holds, full-year spend could reach £45k+.
findings.matters: This signals aging waste infrastructure requiring sustained high revenue replacement spending or capital investment. Council may need to plan for a major capital fleet replacement initiative rather than continue piecemeal replacement from revenue.
findings.figures: Budget £30,000 full year; spend £43,335 to end January; overspend £15,495 (51% overrun through January)
findings.quote: The overspend to date and also against the full year budget reflects an increase in replacement bins issued, which is due to the ageing condition of many of the bins currently in use across the borough.

findings.headline: Refuse collection fleet reliability at risk with £87,061 spent on replacement vehicle hire due to technician vacancy
findings.detail: The council has spent £87,061 by end of January on hiring replacement refuse collection vehicles, with four vehicles alone accounting for £37,863 of overspend. The root cause is a long-standing vacancy in the HGV & Municipal Vehicle Technician post, which means repairs cannot be completed promptly, forcing extended vehicle downtime and emergency hire costs. This represents a statutory service continuity risk.
findings.matters: Refuse collection is a statutory duty. The borough is now dependent on external vehicle hire to maintain service. If the £87,061 spend to end January annualizes, full-year hire costs alone could exceed £104k on top of base repairs budget, representing a major unbudgeted pressure.
findings.figures: £87,061 replacement vehicle hire to end January; £36,203 total vehicle repairs overspend; four vehicles account for £37,863; HGV technician post vacant and re-advertised
findings.quote: The total cost of hiring replacement vehicles for all the refuse collection vehicles up to the end of January 2026 was £87,061. Other significant costs charged to refuse collection vehicles repairs budgets were call out charges, procuring external vehicle technician input for some issues and the costs of parts.

findings.headline: Long-term Works Foreman vacancy and staff sickness driving maintenance cost overruns across multiple council sites
findings.detail: The council has a long-term vacancy in the Works Foreman post and ongoing sickness absence in the Works Team, forcing the council to outsource maintenance work normally done in-house and use external contractors. Remaining team costs are spread over fewer productive hours, inflating hourly rates charged for repairs and maintenance. This cascades into overspends on public conveniences, parks, depots, and car parks.
findings.matters: Indicates inability to retain key infrastructure maintenance staff, creating service delivery risk and poor cost control on a critical support function. If the council cannot staff maintenance adequately, asset condition and service continuity are at risk.
findings.figures: Salthill Depot repairs £8,373 over; Ribble Valley Parks repairs £6,161 over; Car Park Administration £8,616 over; Public Conveniences cleaning £10,213 over
findings.quote: A long-term vacancy and some long-term sickness absence in the Works Team means that employee and other costs of the team are charged out over a lower number of productive hours, thus increasing the costs charged for repair and maintenance work undertaken.

findings.headline: Food Waste Collections scheme will slip into 2027/28; vehicles not expected until summer 2026 at earliest
findings.detail: The £633,840 food waste collections scheme is marked GREEN but vehicles are 'not expected until the summer of 2026 at the earliest' and 'this part of the scheme and the associated budget will move into the next financial year'. Additional depot adaptation costs are expected. Caddies arrive March 2026 but vehicles are TBC.
findings.matters: A service implementation commitment (food waste collections) is now delayed into next year due to procurement timescales. Unbudgeted additional depot spend is expected.
findings.figures: £633,840; caddies delivery March 2026; vehicles delivery TBC (summer 2026 at earliest); additional depot adaptation spend expected
findings.quote: The vehicles and caddies have both been ordered. The caddies should be delivered at the end of March 2026 but the vehicles are not expected until the summer of 2026 at the earliest and therefore this part of the scheme and the associated budget will move into the next financial year. There is also some additional spend expected on adaptation at the depot to make it suitable for handling food waste.

findings.headline: Heritage Lottery bids failed; council approved £794k additional funding for Castle Keep and Castle Grounds
findings.detail: Two major heritage schemes (Castle Keep £399k and Castle Grounds £1.59m) had unsuccessful Heritage Lottery Fund bids in late 2024/early 2025. Policy and Finance Committee approved increased council budgets of £588,820 (Castle Keep, Feb 2025) and £1,792,380 (Castle Grounds, Feb 2025) to cover the shortfall. The council now bears 100% of these scheme costs.
findings.matters: This represents a material increase in council capital commitments (£794k additional) forced by external funding failure. It signals tightened capital discipline and reduced access to grant funding.
findings.figures: Castle Keep budget increase £588,820; Castle Grounds budget increased to £1,792,380 (£204k increase); both bid unsuccessful May 2025
findings.quote: Whilst a Lottery bid for additional funding was unsuccessful, Policy and Finance Committee in February 2025 agreed an overall increased budget of £588, 820... Lottery bid for grant funding was unsuccessful however Policy and Finance Committee, in February 2025, approved an increased budget of £1,792,380.

findings.headline: Longridge 3G Pitch (£1.45m) has slipped from Spring 2025 start and is not yet scoped or designed
findings.detail: The £1.45m Longridge pitch was originally aimed to start Spring 2025. It is now delayed due to Football Foundation discussions to co-fund two additional pitches (Langho and Edisford), creating 'higher level of complexity and scale'. As of March 2026, topographical survey, drainage survey, design, planning application, tendering and contract award are all at 0% completion with no dates assigned.
findings.matters: This is a major capital scheme with significant scope creep from a third-party funder's requirements. No dates are attached to any remaining milestones, creating significant uncertainty about delivery.
findings.figures: £1,446,180; originally Spring 2025 start; all major milestones at 0% completion
findings.quote: since discussions with the Football Foundation, and their proposal to help fund two further pitches at Langho and Edisford using the Council's allocation to match fund, the scheme has taken on a higher level of complexity and scale.

findings.headline: Ribblesdale Pool refurbishment (£4.04m) has no confirmed completion date despite April closure
findings.detail: The £4.04m pool refurbishment is the largest single capital scheme. Pool closes 5 April 2026 but the report lists completion date as 'TBC'. The scheme has already slipped—contract agreement with Alliance Leisure took longer than expected due to legal documentation issues. Design stages show 100% completion but works completion is undefined.
findings.matters: This is 40% of the Community Services capital budget and a major council facility. An undefined completion date for a £4m project creates cash flow uncertainty and operational risk for a leisure service.
findings.figures: £4,037,500; pool closes 5 April 2026; works completion TBC
findings.quote: Pool closes and refurbishment work commences 5 April 2026... Works complete TBC

findings.paper_title: ANNEX 4 - STATEMENT ON THE ROBUSTNESS OF THE ESTIMATES AND BALANCES AND RESERVES
findings.headline: Final Grant Settlement change reduces funding by £466k in 2027/28 and 2028/29 through revised pooling-gain allocation method.
findings.detail: The Local Government Finance Settlement announced a change to pooling gain allocation, moving from the previous methodology to a 50:50 split between tariff and top-up authorities. This policy change directly reduces Ribble Valley's forecast funding by £466k in both 2027/28 and 2028/29—years in which the council already forecasts budget gaps.
findings.matters: Central government policy changes can materially worsen a council's financial position without warning. This £466k reduction arrives directly into a 2027/28 forecast gap of £909k, making an already difficult position significantly harder.
findings.figures: £466k funding reduction in 2027/28 and 2028/29
findings.quote: MHCLG have changed the method to be based on a 50:50 split between tariff and top-up authorities – The impact on this Council is a reduction in funding of £466k in years 2027/28 and 2028/29 compared with our original forecast.

findings.paper_title: ANNEX 4 - STATEMENT ON THE ROBUSTNESS OF THE ESTIMATES AND BALANCES AND RESERVES
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates High/High risk with only £487k provision and no further cost assumption despite minister decision due Summer 2026.
findings.detail: The risk register identifies LGR as high likelihood, high impact. A minister decision on unitary restructuring (2 to 5 unitary councils replacing 15 authorities) is scheduled for Summer 2026 following consultation starting early 2026. However, the budget includes only £487k for transition costs in 2026/27 with no further provision for LGR-related costs.
findings.matters: A major structural reorganisation will generate unfunded transition costs—redundancies, IT systems, process changes—that routinely exceed early estimates. The council is not hedging against a materially uncertain outcome occurring within the budget forecast period.
findings.figures: £487k LGR transition cost provision in 2026/27; no further LGR cost assumption in 2027–2030 forecast
findings.quote: Whilst we have included a provision for transition costs of £487k within the 2026/27 estimates there is no further provision for LGR related costs.

findings.paper_title: ANNEX 4 - STATEMENT ON THE ROBUSTNESS OF THE ESTIMATES AND BALANCES AND RESERVES
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves decline from £13.7m to £3.7m by 2030 to finance the capital programme, removing capital resilience.
findings.detail: The Council plans to deploy £10m of earmarked reserves over four years to finance its capital programme. This heavy reliance on reserves means capital is not self-financing and that available liquidity is continuously depleting.
findings.matters: If capital schemes slip or costs overrun, the council will face external borrowing or further General Fund drawdowns, both of which would worsen the already-forecast deficits. The absence of self-financing capital compounds the structural revenue pressure.
findings.figures: Earmarked Reserves 1 April 2026: £13.698m; projected 1 April 2030: £3.696m
findings.quote: Significant use of our Earmarked Reserves is planned to finance the Council's capital programme 2026/27 to 2029/30. It is therefore estimated the balance of Earmarked Reserves will be £3.696m at 1 April 2030.

findings.paper_title: ANNEX 4 - STATEMENT ON THE ROBUSTNESS OF THE ESTIMATES AND BALANCES AND RESERVES
findings.headline: General Fund Balances fall from £4.6m to £2.1m in 2026/27 through capital scheme withdrawals and council tax freeze funding, leaving minimal buffer.
findings.detail: The Council's main reserve buffer will be depleted by £2.6m in a single year through a £1.24m pool refurbishment, £100k solar panels, £450k cemetery scheme, and £131.85k council tax freeze funding. The S151 Officer notes that the £1m previously considered a minimum level should not be breached without addressing the forecast gaps.
findings.matters: A rapidly shrinking reserve base leaves the council vulnerable to unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. With balances projected to reach £1.33m by 2029/30, only marginally above the historical minimum, the council has minimal resilience to shocks.
findings.quote: However the Budget Forecast predicts large budget gaps beyond 2026/27. It is crucial these are addressed before any further use of General Fund Balances.

findings.paper_title: ANNEX 4 - STATEMENT ON THE ROBUSTNESS OF THE ESTIMATES AND BALANCES AND RESERVES
findings.headline: Budget shortfalls of £909k, £1.29m, and £2.73m forecast for 2027/28 through 2029/30, explicitly flagged by Section 151 Officer as unsustainable.
findings.detail: The Council's four-year forecast predicts increasingly severe budget gaps starting 2026/27, with 2026/27 balanced only through drawing on reserves to fund a council tax freeze. The Section 151 Officer explicitly states these forecast gaps are 'not sustainable' and the Budget Working Group must meet regularly to address them before any further reserve use.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether a council has credible plans to close growing structural deficits. Relying on reserve drawdown signals either underfunded services or budget assumptions that will not hold. Ribble Valley has neither identified solutions nor committed to service reductions.
findings.quote: However, the Council faces significant budget gaps beyond 2027/28. The use of reserves to fund our forecasted budget gaps is not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET 2026/27 AND CAPITAL PROGRAMME 2026/27 – 2029/30 AND SETTING THE COUNCIL TAX FOR EACH CATEGORY OF DWELLING IN THE COUNCIL’S AREA FOR 2026/27
findings.headline: Council has frozen council tax at 2026/27 levels, costing £131,850 in foregone revenue, forcing tighter budgets or faster reserve depletion in future years.
findings.detail: Policy and Finance Committee recommended freezing band D council tax rather than increasing it. This political decision costs £131,850 in 2026/27, met from general fund balances. Forward forecasts assume 2.99% annual increases from 2027/28 onwards, but the freeze this year reduces the base and complicates future planning.
findings.matters: Council tax is the council's most stable, controllable revenue source. Freezing it removes a tool for closing the forward-year deficits and signals political constraints on raising revenue.
findings.figures: £131,850 cost of council tax freeze in 2026/27
findings.quote: ** £131,850 cost of council tax freeze in 2026/27 met from General Fund Balances

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET 2026/27 AND CAPITAL PROGRAMME 2026/27 – 2029/30 AND SETTING THE COUNCIL TAX FOR EACH CATEGORY OF DWELLING IN THE COUNCIL’S AREA FOR 2026/27
findings.headline: Government grant settlement changed dramatically mid-cycle, cutting Ribble Valley's funding by £466k annually via business rates reallocation, partly masked by one-off support.
findings.detail: The final grant settlement reversed the provisional allocation of business rates pooling gains, moving from a 100% allocation to tariff authorities to a 50:50 split with top-up authorities. This cost Ribble Valley £466k in forgone Revenue Support Grant and Damping Payment. A one-off Adjustment Support Grant of £466k was awarded for 2026/27 only, masking the permanent hit.
findings.matters: Unexpected mid-year grant cuts reveal vulnerability to government funding volatility. The one-off mitigation ends in 2027/28, creating a hidden cliff edge in future years.
findings.figures: £466k annual impact; Revenue Support Grant reduced from £3.525m to £3.191m; Damping Payment reduced from £195k to £62k
findings.quote: This is reflected in our reduced Revenue Support Grant (was £3.525m now £3.191m) and also our reduced Damping Payment (was £195k now £62k).

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET 2026/27 AND CAPITAL PROGRAMME 2026/27 – 2029/30 AND SETTING THE COUNCIL TAX FOR EACH CATEGORY OF DWELLING IN THE COUNCIL’S AREA FOR 2026/27
findings.headline: General fund balances will halve in a single year, falling from £4.646m to £2.079m, leaving minimal headroom above the Section 151 Officer's £1m minimum.
findings.detail: The council will draw down £2.29m from general fund balances for capital investment and £277k for revenue in 2026/27. The Section 151 Officer judges that 'in such times of uncertainty, the minimum level should be £1m', meaning the council will have only £1.079m of discretionary headroom to absorb shocks.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves reduce the council's ability to manage in-year variances or unexpected costs. A lender views reserves as essential shock absorbers and signs of financial discipline.
findings.figures: Opening 2025/26: £4.082m; forecast 31 March 2026: £4.646m; after 2026/27 drawdowns: £2.079m
findings.quote: my view, in such times of uncertainty, is that the minimum level should be £1m. Estimated Balances in Hand 31 March 2026 2,079

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET 2026/27 AND CAPITAL PROGRAMME 2026/27 – 2029/30 AND SETTING THE COUNCIL TAX FOR EACH CATEGORY OF DWELLING IN THE COUNCIL’S AREA FOR 2026/27
findings.headline: Forecast budget shortfalls of £909k (2027/28), £1.29m (2028/29), and £2.73m (2029/30) cannot be sustainably funded from reserves.
findings.detail: The council's Section 151 Officer explicitly states that while the 2026/27 budget is balanced, forward projections show growing deficits. The officer warns that 'the use of reserves to fund our forecasted budget gaps is not sustainable' and calls for urgent Budget Working Group action to address shortfalls from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council can meet its obligations beyond the current year. Structural deficits that outpace reserve drawdown signal deteriorating financial resilience.
findings.quote: The Council faces significant budget gaps beyond 2027/28. The use of reserves to fund our forecasted budget gaps is not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: 100226 revenue budget specpf - addendum Agenda item 6 100226
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves also declining significantly, from £13.698m to £3.696m over four years
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves (set aside for specific purposes) fall by more than 70% over the forecast period, from £13.7m to £3.7m. Combined with general fund depletion, this represents a wholesale drawdown of the council's contingency and strategic capacity.
findings.matters: Both reserve categories are being depleted. A lender needs confidence that the council retains adequate reserves for service continuity, audit requirements, and unexpected costs. The trajectory suggests none of these will be adequately covered by 2029/30.
findings.figures: Balance at Earmarked Reserves: 31/03/2026 £13.698m → 31/03/2030 £3.696m (73% reduction over 4 years).
findings.quote: Closing balances based on budget forecast: Balance at Earmarked Reserves 31/03/2026 13.698m 31/03/2030 3.696m

findings.paper_title: 100226 revenue budget specpf - addendum Agenda item 6 100226
findings.headline: Audit recommendations from Value for Money assessment present but details not disclosed in this addendum
findings.detail: Section 3.5 reports that Grant Thornton (external auditor) made recommendations during a recent Value for Money assessment, but the document shows only a heading and blank space. The specific recommendations and any weaknesses identified are not visible in this version.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know what audit concerns exist and whether they relate to financial controls, reserve adequacy, or other material weaknesses. Omission of detail is a red flag.
findings.figures: None provided.
findings.quote: During our recent Value For Money (VFM) assessment, our external auditors, Grant Thornton, made the following recommendations.

findings.paper_title: 100226 revenue budget specpf - addendum Agenda item 6 100226
findings.headline: Funding settlement changes: pooling gains reallocation costs £466k p.a., worse than expected from provisional settlement
findings.detail: Government changed the business rates pooling gains allocation mid-settlement, moving from 100% retention by tariff authorities (Ribble Valley's position) to 50/50 split with top-up authorities. This does not match how the Lancashire pool actually operates (10/90 split). The council lost £466k in annual funding as a result, and whilst protected for one year, faces this loss from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: This shows government funding rules shifting mid-year and the council's actual income position deteriorating during the spending year, not improving. It signals that the council's assumptions about business rates income and pooling benefits may be fragile.
findings.figures: Reduction in Revenue Support Grant: £3.525m (provisional) to £3.191m (final), a £334k drop. Reduction in Damping Payment: £195k (provisional) to £62k (final), a £133k drop. Total impact: £466k per year.
findings.quote: This does not reflect the reality of how the Lancashire Business Rate Pool operated whereby 10% of retained levies (the income saved by pooling) were paid to the top-up authority and 90% retained by the tariff authorities.

findings.paper_title: 100226 revenue budget specpf - addendum Agenda item 6 100226
findings.headline: General Fund Balances depleted from £4.646m to £2.211m in one budget cycle, and scheduled to fall further to £1.461m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The council is drawing £2.44m from reserves in 2026/27 alone (£145,821 for revenue shortfall plus £2.29m for capital projects: pool refurbishment £1.24m, solar panels £100k, cemetery extension £450k, market/joiners arms improvements £500k). The forecast then uses a further £750k (£250k p.a. for three years) to support operating deficits, leaving reserves barely adequate and creating no buffer for further surprises.
findings.matters: Reserves are being consumed to fund both recurrent service spending and capital projects, not being held as a genuine contingency. The downward trajectory leaves the council increasingly exposed if costs rise or income falls short.
findings.figures: Closing General Fund Balance: 31/03/2026 actual £4.646m → 31/03/2027 forecast £2.211m → 31/03/2030 forecast £1.461m. Capital drawdowns in 2026/27: £1.24m + £100k + £450k + £500k = £2.29m.
findings.quote: Taken to support Pool scheme -1,240,000 Taken to fund Ribblesdale Pool Solar Panels -100,000 Taken to fund Clitheroe Cemetery Capital Scheme -450,000 Taken to fund Joiners Arms/Market Improvements -500,000 Carried Forward 2,210,633

findings.paper_title: 100226 revenue budget specpf - addendum Agenda item 6 100226
findings.headline: Cliff edge at end of damping period: £466k annual funding loss from 2027/28 onwards after one-year protection ends
findings.detail: The council received a one-off Adjustment Support Grant of £466k in 2026/27 to offset the impact of changed business rates pooling rules at the final settlement. This protection expires. The council's core funding (Revenue Support Grant plus damping) then drops sharply. Damping protection ends entirely by 2029/30, creating the budget catastrophe then.
findings.matters: The one-off grant masks the depth of the structural problem. A lender seeing a balanced budget for 2026/27 might not spot that year 2 onwards is in deficit with no identified savings plan and that year 4 has a catastrophic £2.58m gap.
findings.figures: Adjustment Support Grant: £466k in 2026/27 only; £0 in 2027/28 and 2028/29. Damping Payment drops from £62k in 2026/27 to £667k in 2027/28 to £1.29m in 2028/29 before vanishing.
findings.quote: The significant increase in the budget gap in 2029/30 represents the 'cliff edge' at the end of the 3 year multi settlement when our damping protection will cease.

findings.paper_title: 100226 revenue budget specpf - addendum Agenda item 6 100226
findings.headline: Structural budget deficits of £772k and £1.15m in years 2 and 3, reaching £2.58m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The council has balanced 2026/27 using a one-off Adjustment Support Grant and council tax increases. However, the medium-term forecast shows deficits widening sharply. From 2027/28 onwards, the council lacks funding solutions for the gaps and is using reserves as a stopgap. The Section 151 officer explicitly states this approach is unsustainable.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has a credible medium-term plan to close these deficits or whether it is burning reserves and has no structured path back to balance.
findings.figures: 2027/28: £771,991 gap; 2028/29: £1,147,520 gap; 2029/30: £2,584,718 gap. All figures after drawing £250k per year from reserves and assuming 2.99% annual council tax increases.
findings.quote: Whilst the level of General Fund Balances and Earmarked Reserves is relatively high, the use of reserves to fund our budget gaps would not prove sufficient to cover the forecast deficits and would not be sustainable.

findings.headline: Audit recommendations from prior years remain outstanding; internal audit capacity crisis makes timely implementation impossible.
findings.detail: Multiple audit recommendations from 2022/23 and 2023/24 remain unimplemented (ICT security policy, procurement strategy, risk management enhancements). With only 1 of 3 internal audit positions filled as of September 2025 (despite two recruitment attempts), the council lacks capacity to either conduct risk-based audits or track implementation of prior recommendations. Auditors noted the original 2024/25 audit plan included 14 audits, but not all were completed.
findings.matters: Unimplemented audit recommendations represent identified control gaps that remain unaddressed. A weakened internal audit team cannot identify new risks or enforce accountability for fixing old ones, leaving the council's control environment progressively weaker.
findings.figures: Internal audit team: 1 of 3 positions filled (as of September 2025); 64 audit recommendations under review for implementation; multiple recommendations marked overdue from prior audits (including 2-3 from 2022/23); original 2024/25 audit plan of 14 audits not fully delivered.
findings.quote: As of September 2025, only one member of the internal audit team (out of three positions) was in post, despite the Council making two attempts to recruit. We note that the original audit plan included 14 audits, however not all were completed.

findings.headline: Contract register not updated for 18 months; 30 expired contracts remain on record with no exceptions reported to audit committee.
findings.detail: The council's contract register was last updated in March 2024 and has not been refreshed since. It contains 30 contracts marked as expired, 27 of which expired during 2024/25. Auditors found no evidence that exceptions to contract standing orders were reported to the Accounts and Audit Committee in 2024/25. This indicates a breakdown in contract lifecycle management and monitoring.
findings.matters: An out-of-date contract register obscures the council's actual contractual commitments, liabilities, and payment obligations. It creates risk of unmonitored contractors continuing to invoice, undetected breaches of contract terms, and incomplete asset/liability records.
findings.figures: Contract register not updated since March 2024 (18 months stale); 30 expired contracts on record; 27 of those expired during 2024/25.
findings.quote: The Council has not updated its contract register since March 2024, and it currently includes 30 expired contracts, 27 of which expired during 2024/25.

findings.headline: Multiple regulatory and compliance failures: CIPFA code self-assessment not started, policies severely out of date, transparency code requirements not met.
findings.detail: The council has made no progress on a self-assessment against the CIPFA Financial Management Code due to capacity issues. The Information Technology Security Policy was last updated in 2015 (10 years old). The staff code of conduct was last reviewed in 2012 (13 years old). The member code of conduct was last updated in 2021. Not all councillor declarations of interest are current. The council is also not meeting Local Government Transparency Code 2015 requirements.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with regulatory codes and failure to maintain current policies indicates a governance culture that does not prioritise compliance. Out-of-date policies leave the council exposed to control failures and risks that haven't been reassessed in years.
findings.figures: CIPFA code assessment: not started as of September 2025; IT Security Policy: last updated 2015; staff code of conduct: last reviewed 2012; policies identified as out of date in 2023/24 Annual Governance Statement remained unchanged in 2024/25.
findings.quote: Our work has identified several areas where the Council is not ensuring the appropriate standards and meeting regulatory requirements. In 2024/25 and up to September 2025, the Council made no progress on a self-assessment against the CIPFA financial management code due to capacity.

findings.headline: Ribblesdale Pool capital scheme facing 40% cost overrun, from £3m budget to £4.2m forecast.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget approved £3m for an upgrade to Ribblesdale Pool. In May 2025, the Community Services Committee was advised that actual costs are likely to increase to £4.2m — a £1.2m overspend. Auditors flagged they will review this scheme and examine the reporting and programme management in place as part of their 2025/26 VFM work.
findings.matters: A major capital project running 40% over budget indicates weak project controls, scope creep, or estimation failures. It will force the council to either find additional funding, draw on reserves, or reallocate resources from other priorities.
findings.figures: Original budget £3m; revised forecast £4.2m (increase of £1.2m or 40%).
findings.quote: In May 2025 we note the Community Services Committee was advised the cost of the Pool was likely to increase to £4.2m.

findings.headline: Significant weakness in performance management — council cannot track whether services are delivering value, and auditors may exercise statutory powers if no improvement is seen.
findings.detail: Auditors identified a significant weakness (red flag rating) in the council's performance management arrangements. The council has made limited progress since 2022/23 on implementing a performance framework, and this has been further constrained by capacity issues from Local Government Reorganisation preparation. As of September 2025, KPI targets and baselines have still not been agreed; reporting is delayed and limited. Auditors explicitly stated: 'Given the lack of movement in progressing our audit recommendations, progress will be closely monitored and if sustained improvement is not seen, particularly in the context of preparations for LGR, we will consider exercising our auditor statutory powers.'
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council can track whether services are delivering value and can identify inefficiencies or problems that need fixing. Without robust performance data and the ability to respond to findings, the council cannot demonstrate it is managing taxpayers' money effectively.
findings.figures: Only 1 of 3 internal audit positions filled (as of September 2025, despite two recruitment attempts); Management Performance Framework not submitted to committee until after 2024/25 year-end; new KPI set had no targets or baselines agreed; Q1 and Q2 reporting on 40 new KPIs planned to start October 2025 (now in progress).
findings.quote: During 2024/25, the capacity issues at the Council were further constrained by preparation for the Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) process and therefore we note that this situation continued into 2025/26. We note that a Management Performance Framework has been taken to Policy and Finance Committee with proposed KPIs and reporting against corporate plan and service levels, this was not during 2024/25, hence we retain our key recommendation.

findings.headline: Recruitment difficulties in Planning team impacting Local Plan delivery
findings.detail: The Planning Policy team has experienced ongoing recruitment difficulties that continued to impact delivery of the new Local Plan for 2028–2038. The council addressed recruitment needs 'throughout the year' but the impact on service delivery was not resolved.
findings.matters: Staffing pressures on strategic service delivery are a sign of wider labour market and retention challenges. Delays to statutory planning documents can affect the council's ability to attract investment and control development-related financial pressures.
findings.figures: Planning Policy team; new Local Plan period: 2028–2038
findings.quote: Ongoing recruitment difficulties in the Planning Policy team continued to impact the delivery of the new Local Plan (for the period 2028-2038), however the Council actively addressed recruitment needs throughout the year.

findings.headline: Staff performance appraisal process momentum lapsed during 2024/25
findings.detail: Appraisals were restarted in 2023/24 after COVID disruption but 'the impetus in this area fell during 2024/25,' indicating the council did not sustain this governance control. This suggests HR and performance management processes are not embedded as routine practice.
findings.matters: Lapsed appraisals indicate weak governance discipline on HR controls and suggest that staffing issues or performance problems may not be identified or addressed early.
findings.figures: Process momentum fell during 2024/25
findings.quote: Staff appraisals recommenced in 2023/24 (following Covid-19); however, the impetus in this area fell during 2024/25.

findings.headline: Operational risk management system remains incomplete; services not documenting risks
findings.detail: Despite being flagged as an action item in 2023/24, the operational risk management system still lacks input from multiple service areas. Some service-level risks have been uploaded to the risk management system, but 'other services are yet to formally document their operational risks.' The statement flags this will continue into 2025/26.
findings.matters: An incomplete risk register means the council may not have visibility of emerging service-level pressures, particularly financial risks or capacity constraints that could impact financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Status: 'Partially Implemented'; continuation flagged for 2025/26
findings.quote: Although some service-level operational risks have been uploaded on to the risk management system, other services are yet to formally document their operational risks.

findings.headline: Auditor identified material weakness in performance management that remains unresolved
findings.detail: The 2023/24 audit report recommended the council 'ensure it had the capacity to significantly improve its performance management arrangements' and suggested specific measures. The governance statement acknowledges that while 'many of these measures are now in place,' preparation for local government reorganisation has constrained capacity, implying the improvements are incomplete and at risk.
findings.matters: Poor performance management increases the risk that financial or operational problems are not detected in real time. This was flagged as a material audit concern and remains only partially remedied.
findings.figures: Auditor recommendation from 2023/24; key recommendation status: 'work progressing on those items not yet completed'
findings.quote: A key recommendation from the Auditor's Report 2023/24 was for the Council to ensure it had the capacity to significantly improve its performance management arrangements, suggesting a number of specific measures in order to achieve this. Although preparation for LGR has constrained capacity somewhat, many of these measures are now in place with work progressing on those items not yet completed.

findings.headline: Multiple governance compliance issues from prior year remain only partially implemented
findings.detail: Three governance issues carried forward from 2023/24—policy review and ratification, Health and Safety risk assessments, and operational risk documentation—remain marked as 'Partially Implemented' after a full year. The statement acknowledges 'progress has been made in the areas that have been carried forward, but actions need to continue to fully address the issues raised.'
findings.matters: Recurring governance control issues suggest either insufficient priority or capacity to embed core controls. For a lender, this indicates the control environment is not tightening and poses longer-term governance risk.
findings.figures: 3 governance actions marked 'Partially Implemented' in both 2023/24 and 2024/25
findings.quote: Although progress has been made in the areas that have been carried forward, actions need to continue to fully address the issues raised.

findings.headline: s151 Officer split across Chief Executive duties for 2.5 days per week throughout 2024/25
findings.detail: Due to senior management changes, the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive (the council's chief financial officer) was undertaking interim Chief Executive responsibilities for 2.5 days per week alongside their existing finance role for the entire financial year. This dual role arrangement means the council's financial leadership was not focused full-time on financial stewardship.
findings.matters: Lenders need confidence that the chief financial officer has dedicated capacity and focus to manage the council's finances and respond to emerging financial pressures. A split role raises questions about whether financial decision-making and monitoring were compromised.
findings.figures: 2½ days per week throughout 2024/25
findings.quote: Senior Management changes resulted in the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive undertaking the extra duties of Chief Executive 2½ days per week, alongside their existing role, throughout 2024/25.

findings.headline: Asset valuation data error resulted in £76k understatement of land and buildings
findings.detail: Floor plans provided to the external valuer did not match the areas actually used in the valuation, creating an unadjusted misstatement where land and buildings are understated by £76k across the council's £16.06m asset base.
findings.matters: Though relatively small against total assets, the error points to incomplete control over asset data accuracy; similar errors could exist elsewhere.
findings.figures: £76k unadjusted misstatement; total land and buildings valuation £16.06m
findings.quote: We identified that some of the floor plans provided to support the areas used by the external valuer in valuing the Council's land and buildings did not match the areas applied by the valuer this has resulted in an unadjusted misstatement of £76k

findings.headline: Segregation of duties control weakness: finance officer holds both transaction posting authority and system superuser access
findings.detail: The Head of Financial Services can post journals and also holds superuser system access, creating a control deficiency where unauthorized or inappropriate entries could be posted or system permissions altered without independent review.
findings.matters: This control gap creates a risk of undetected fraud or error; lenders rely on segregation of duties as a core financial control.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The Head of Financial Services has both journal posting authority and superuser system access. This creates a risk that unauthorised or inappropriate entries could be posted, or system permissions altered, without independent review. This combination of access constitutes a control weakness, and we regard it as a segregation of duties deficiency.

findings.headline: Significant weakness identified in value for money arrangements regarding performance management and organizational capacity
findings.detail: The auditor is not satisfied that the council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. The report explicitly states that if sustained improvement is not achieved in performance management, the auditor will consider exercising statutory powers.
findings.matters: A VFM significant weakness means the council has governance deficiencies that could impair its ability to improve or implement changes; auditor exercise of statutory powers is a material governance escalation.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: We identified a significant weakness(s) in the Council's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.headline: Weekly food waste collection (£600k cost) may not be funded if the government rolls new burdens grants into core funding settlements.
findings.detail: The council assumes the £600k cost of mandatory weekly food waste collection will be covered by new burdens grant. However, recent information suggests this funding may be 'rolled in' to general grant settlements, meaning the money will not arrive separately and the true burden will not be funded. The council will not know until December.
findings.matters: A £600k unfunded cost could force service reductions elsewhere. This is a direct mandate-funding mismatch that creates budget risk.
findings.figures: £600k estimated cost for weekly food waste collection
findings.quote: We have assumed to date that the introduction of the weekly collection of food waste estimated to cost £600k will be funded from new burdens grant. Alarmingly recent information suggests that new burdens funding will be rolled in to grant settlements. We won't know until the settlement is announced in December.

findings.headline: The budget forecast explicitly excludes the impact of a potential leisure pool closure and resulting loss of income.
findings.detail: The council notes that the budget forecast 'does not take into account any consequences of the capital programme including the potential pool closure and hence loss of income.' This is a material item affecting both capital and revenue budgets that is not modeled.
findings.matters: A pool closure would generate both capital disposal gains and revenue income losses. The exclusion of this from the forecast means the true 2026-29 budget position is incomplete and potentially worse than modeled.
findings.figures: Impact of pool closure not quantified in the forecast
findings.quote: This budget forecast assumes that any proposed growth items will be funded from identified sayings and/or new burdens funding.
