At this stage the budget forecast does not take into account any consequences of the capital programme including the potential pool closure and hence loss of income.

findings.headline: The council cannot properly forecast revenue for 2026-29 because the government has not provided exemplifications or detailed funding information.
findings.detail: Despite fundamental changes to local government funding through Fair Funding 2.0, the government has not issued any exemplifications showing the impact on individual councils. The council explicitly states it will not know detailed funding until the Provisional Finance Settlement in December, leaving a two-month planning window before the financial year begins.
findings.matters: This creates material planning risk. Budget forecasts become guesswork. Service committees are being asked to plan savings and growth without knowing the true funding envelope. The council acknowledges this is a 'draft Budget Forecast which will be updated as more information becomes available.'
findings.figures: Policy Statement expected end September/early October; Provisional Settlement not until December; financial year begins April 2026
findings.quote: despite these fundamental changes, the Government have not issued any exemplifications which would show the potential impact of each of the proposals on each Council. There is no indication we will learn of our detailed funding before the Provisional Finance Settlement is announced which is not until usually just before Christmas.

findings.headline: Pension employer contribution rate is unknown and will change from 2026/27, with the new rate not yet determined.
findings.detail: A triennial review of the Lancashire Pensions Fund was completed on 31 March 2025, with new employer contributions effective from 2026/27. The current rate is 14.7%. The council states it is 'due to attend meetings with the Pensions administrator in the coming weeks' to learn the new rate, but has made no assumption for this in the forecast.
findings.matters: Pension costs are material (total payroll is £9.379m) and any increase would worsen the budget deficit. The omission of the new contribution rate from the forecast means the true budget position is unknown.
findings.figures: Current employer contribution rate 14.7%; total payroll £9.379m
findings.quote: A triennial pension review of the Lancashire Pensions Fund took place on 31 March 2025 with changes to our employer's pension contributions being effective from 2026/27. Our current contribution rate is 14.7%. We are due to attend meetings with the Pensions administrator in the coming weeks where we hope to learn more about the overall position on the pensions fund and of our new contribution rate.

findings.headline: The council is drawing down £250k annually from general fund balances to balance the budget, depleting reserves without a recovery plan.
findings.detail: The three-year forecast assumes the council will use £250k from general balances each year to bridge the projected budget gaps. This is a structural deficit being covered by reserve depletion rather than sustainable savings.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite. This approach is unsustainable beyond a few years and signals the council cannot balance its budget through service provision alone. Lenders assess reserve position as a key indicator of financial resilience.
findings.figures: £250k per year for three years = £750k total reserve depletion
findings.quote: assume we will use £0.25m from general balances each year

findings.headline: Investment income is declining by 75% over three years, from £1m to £250k, due to expected interest rate falls.
findings.detail: The council currently benefits significantly from holding £30m invested on the money markets, generating £1m annually in 2025/26. However, the forecast assumes interest rates will fall from 4% to 3.5-3.7%, reducing investment returns to £750k, £500k, and £250k in successive years.
findings.matters: This is a major income loss (£750k annually by 2028/29) driven by macro factors outside the council's control. Combined with other income losses, it exacerbates the budget gap.
findings.quote: We have currently approx. £30m invested on the money markets. We anticipate our investment interest for 2025/26 will be £1m... we have assumed the following returns on our investments over the life of the forecast: 2026/27 £750k, 2027/28 £500k, 2028/29 £250k

findings.headline: Business rate growth baseline will be reset in 2026/27, eliminating the council's ability to estimate or plan for this income.
findings.detail: The council currently relies on £2m of business rate growth annually to support the revenue budget. However, with the baseline reset confirmed, the council explicitly states it 'cannot estimate how much business rate growth (if any) we will receive' from 2026/27 onwards. Business rate growth currently makes up 18% of the budget.
findings.matters: The council loses £2m in planned revenue, cannot forecast a replacement, and loses a key lever for managing budget pressures. Lenders need to understand this income is now unpredictable.
findings.figures: Currently £2.7m total business rate growth; £2m supporting revenue budget; £500k funding capital
findings.quote: it has now been confirmed that business rates baselines will be reset therefore we cannot estimate how much business rate growth (if any) we will receive from next year at this stage.

findings.headline: Budget gaps of £937k, £1.5m, and £2.1m over the next three years with no identified funding solution.
findings.detail: The council's three-year forecast, based on assumed 5-7% funding reduction in 2026/27 followed by a cash freeze, shows cumulative deficits growing each year. The forecast assumes £250k drawdown from general balances annually to bridge these gaps, but no savings plan or service reduction strategy is outlined.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to know where £2.1m in savings will come from by 2028/29; a lender needs to know whether reserves can sustain these annual drawdowns or whether the council will be forced into service cuts.
findings.quote: If we factor these Core Spending Power figures into the latest three-year budget forecast and assume we will use £0.25m from general balances each year, the budget gaps are as follows: 2026/27 937k, 2027/28 1,537k, 2028/29 2,147k

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Activities and Prudential Indicators 2024/25
findings.headline: Capital programme slipped by £1.3m, mostly into 2025/26
findings.detail: Against a revised capital estimate of £3.36m (excluding UK Shared Prosperity Fund schemes), the council spent only £2.05m. The paper states that 'the majority of which related to slippage on several schemes into the 2025/26 capital programme.' Community Services, Health and Housing, and Policy and Finance all significantly underspent their revised budgets.
findings.matters: Capital slippage signals project delivery risk. A lender needs to know whether a council can execute its plans on schedule, and whether deferred schemes will create cash flow pressure in following years.
findings.figures: Revised estimate £3.36m, actual outturn £2.05m, variance £1.31m underspend
findings.quote: based on the outturn position there was an underspend variance against the revised estimate of £1,311,922, the majority of which related to slippage on several schemes into the 2025/26 capital programme

findings.headline: Economic Development Committee tracking to £36,863 overspend after four months
findings.detail: Net cost of services already in £36,863 overspend to end July 2025, driven by Albion Mill issues. This represents 10% of the committee's full-year net budget of £362,050.
findings.matters: Shows material budget control issue early in financial year with significant unquantified costs still to come; trajectory suggests substantial full-year overspend.
findings.figures: £36,863 overspend; committee net budget £362,050 full year
findings.quote: You will see an overall overspend of £36,863 on the net cost of services.

findings.headline: Albion Mill vacancy-related costs for utilities, service charges and professional fees still uncharted
findings.detail: Gas, electricity, service charges, solicitor consent fees, and cleaning costs from vacant periods and re-letting remain to be invoiced. These costs do not appear in the current report because actual charges have not yet been received.
findings.matters: Reported figures are incomplete; actual outturn will be materially worse than currently shown, making the £36,863 committee overspend a floor, not a ceiling.
findings.figures: Not yet quantified in the report
findings.quote: The Council will incur additional costs from the vacant periods and re-letting of the three units referred to above, in relation to gas and electricity, service charges, solicitors consent fees and cleaning costs. The actual costs in most of these areas are still to be charged to the Council, so do not appear in this report.

findings.headline: £20,542 former tenant arrears from Albion Mill difficult to collect, with one tenant owing £20,193
findings.detail: Arrears from prior years with collection problems acknowledged. One former tenant accounts for £20,193 of the total. Options for recovery are still being considered with no agreed path forward documented.
findings.matters: Suggests structural collection risk on the council's commercial tenancy portfolio and potential cash flow impact.
findings.figures: £20,542 total arrears; £20,193 from single tenant
findings.quote: Former tenants arrears of £20,542 from previous years and these have been difficult to collect so far.

findings.headline: Council incurring £7,735 NNDR (business rates) liability on vacant Albion Mill units
findings.detail: As landlord, the council is liable for NNDR on units that become vacant. Three units vacant April-July 2025 triggered unexpected business rates costs. The amount shown covers only units 2 and 3; unit 1 vacancy costs will be added once invoiced.
findings.matters: Unexpected liability arising from asset vacancy; actual exposure is larger than currently reported and will increase further.
findings.figures: £7,735 to date (units 2 and 3 only); unit 1 costs to be added
findings.quote: The Council, as landlord, is liable for the NNDR on any units that become vacant in-year. Three of the five units at Albion Mill have been vacant between April and July 2025, meaning there is a NNDR liability for the Council in-year.

findings.headline: Albion Mill rent income £33,017 below budget due to three units vacant since April 2025
findings.detail: Original budget assumed full occupancy of five units. Units 1, 2 and 3 have been vacant between April and July 2025. New leases were expected to be agreed in March 2025 but remain pending consent from the underlease holder due to disagreement over tenant LTA protection clauses.
findings.matters: A council-owned revenue asset is significantly underperforming against budget assumptions, with recovery dependent on resolving disputes with a third-party underlease holder.
findings.figures: £33,017 rent income under-recovery to end July 2025; three of five units vacant
findings.quote: Three of the five units at Albion Mill have been vacant between April and July 2025, which was not expected when the original estimate budget was set.

findings.headline: Unexpected service cost increase for housing waiting list management
findings.detail: Onward Homes has substantially increased its annual charge for managing the council's housing waiting list compared to previous years' costs used in budget setting. The increase was not anticipated when the budget was set, but has been accepted as an unavoidable cost necessary to maintain the service.
findings.matters: A core contracted service cost has increased significantly with no identified offset, representing an unbudgeted cost pressure on the housing service.
findings.figures: £4,664 variance on Housing Strategy budget; described as 'substantial price increase'
findings.quote: The increase in the Onward Homes charge to manage the housing waiting list is accepted as a necessary cost of the service.

findings.headline: Unresolved refund liabilities to former temporary housing tenants
findings.detail: The council owes refunds to previous tenants of Joiners Arms temporary accommodation for overpaid rent relating to multiple prior years. Despite efforts to locate the tenants, they have been difficult to contact, leaving these liabilities unresolved. The report identifies this as unlikely to be settled by year end, with the organisation currently undertaking discussions on how to manage the approach to refunds and arrears.
findings.matters: This represents an unquantified contingent liability and indicates governance or operational weaknesses in managing temporary housing accounts and tenant contact records.
findings.figures: £2,938 refund variance recorded in year to date; amounts relate to previous financial years
findings.quote: The Council owes refunds to a number of previous tenants for over paid rent. Despite efforts to issue refunds the tenants have been difficult to locate.

findings.headline: Affordable housing income loss due to property renovation and lease completion delays
findings.detail: A property at 61 Peel Street intended as affordable housing, with income budgeted from April 2025, has not generated any rental income to date. Renovation work proved more extensive than anticipated and the lease agreement with Onward Homes has not been completed. The council will now receive only 50% of the budgeted rental income for 2025/26, with income expected to resume in September.
findings.matters: A material revenue income source has failed to materialize as planned, and recovery depends on successful completion of both renovation and lease execution.
findings.figures: £6,326 annual revenue variance (50% of budgeted income lost for the year)
findings.quote: The delay in preparing the property and the lease means that 50% of in the rental income budgeted for in 2025/26 will not be achieved.

findings.headline: Purchase of Affordable Housing scheme has zero progress; delivery strategy contingent on unspecified Section 106 funding timeline
findings.detail: A £500K scheme (12% of the program) shows £0 spend and £0 commitment. The council's plan is to prioritise Section 106 monies (developer contributions) first, then decide how to spend its own capital, but no timescale or criteria for that decision are offered.
findings.matters: A half-million-pound budget line with no forward plan raises questions about capital prioritisation and timing risk; dependence on external developer contributions creates a funding dependency outside the council's control.
findings.figures: Budget £500,000; spend £0; Amber status with milestone dates October 2025 onwards
findings.quote: This will note the necessity to focus on schemes funded by Section 106 monies first as these are time sensitive. Officers will need to consider options for the capital funding with the Working Group once all of the S106 monies have been committed.

findings.headline: Legal advice blocked Assisted Purchase model entirely; scheme pivoted to different delivery model
findings.detail: The £422K Assisted Purchase scheme's original model (helping first-time buyers with deposits) has been ruled out by Trowers legal advice. The council is now pivoting to buying and renovating a council-owned property for affordable rent instead. All key milestones show 0% progress with target completion in October 2025.
findings.matters: Mid-year pivots on significant schemes reflect planning risk or external constraints the council did not anticipate; the new model (council property ownership and management) carries different financial and operational risks than the original scheme.
findings.figures: Budget £421,970; spend £200,800 (47.6%); scheme completion now contingent on Oct 2025 survey and Registered Provider agreement
findings.quote: A report to January H & H Committee set out legal advice received from Trowers which did not support delivering the model of assisting first time buyers with a deposit but suggested investigating a shared equity model. This is no longer an option.

findings.headline: Affordable Housing Longridge scheme stalled with lead delivery partner unresponsive
findings.detail: The council's largest single capital scheme (£1.08M, 27% of total program) has managed only £1,500 spend (0.1%) by July. The council reports no communication from Onward, the housing association meant to deliver it, and is now pivoting to unspecified alternative proposals. No revised delivery timeline is offered.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council can execute on significant capital commitments; radio silence from a lead partner on a major scheme, with the original plan abandoned mid-year, signals execution risk.
findings.figures: Budget £1,082,730; spend £1,500 (0.1%); scheme represents 27% of total approved capital program
findings.quote: We have received no feedback from Onward and therefore, given the timeframes, we have reported to Committee alternative proposals for the spend of this capital scheme.

findings.headline: Planning Policy vacancies causing salary underspend above normal turnover assumptions
findings.detail: Multiple salary and on-cost budgets show underspends attributed to vacancies within the Planning Policy section of the Economic Development and Planning department, totalling around £28,000 in salary, national insurance, and superannuation underspends. These exceed the 4% turnover built into budget estimates and are flagged as unlikely to rectify by year-end.
findings.matters: Unexpectedly high vacancies above normal turnover could indicate recruitment challenges, service delivery risk, or retention issues. The paper does not clarify whether these are planned or unexpected, or how long positions have been vacant.
findings.figures: ECPLA salaries underspend £20,991; ECPLA national insurance underspend £3,772; ECPLA superannuation underspend £3,463; LPLAN salary underspend £11,282
findings.quote: Vacancy underspends are higher than the 4% turnover built into the budget estimate, mainly due to vacancies within the Planning Policy Section.

findings.headline: Planning fee income is 7.3% below budget in Q1 with no forecast recovery
findings.detail: The council budgeted £137,403 in planning fee income for the three months to June 2025 but received only £127,363, a shortfall of £10,040. The council notes that planning income fluctuates depending on whether major development applications are received. The shortfall is not flagged for recovery by year-end and will be reviewed at revised estimate.
findings.matters: Planning fees are discretionary income that varies significantly with development activity. A 7% shortfall in Q1 could annualise to £40k+ if major applications don't materialise, putting pressure on the revenue budget.
findings.figures: Budget £137,403, actual £127,363, variance £10,040 (Q1); full-year budget £549,180
findings.quote: Planning income levels fluctuate month to month and vary greatly depending on whether applications are received in respect of major developments over the year and within the financial period.

news_drafts.headline: Over £360k in grant funding received but not yet spent may force a reserve drawdown if not expended in year.
news_drafts.lead: Grant-funded spend that carries forward creates a reserve liability. If the council cannot spend this funding in-year, it creates a commitment that reduces future financial flexibility.

news_drafts.headline: Environmental Health externally sources statutory inspection work because the council has no qualified staff, and this overspend will repeat.
news_drafts.lead: A council unable to resource statutory functions internally faces recurring budget pressure and potential service risk. This is a structural problem, not a one-off variance.

news_drafts.headline: Clitheroe Market maintenance is running 83% over budget four months in and is unlikely to recover.
news_drafts.lead: Reactive maintenance running over budget suggests either deferred maintenance or an asset in poor condition. Either way, this indicates future capital or revenue pressure.
